The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

To determine the final state of the numbers on the board, we must analyze the effect of the operation $a, b \to \gcd(a, b), \operatorname{lcm}(a, b)$.

### Step 1: Analyze the Invariant and Final State

Let the set of numbers on the board be $S$. The product of all numbers in $S$ is invariant under the operation because $\gcd(a,b)\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = ab$.
More importantly, consider the prime factorization of the numbers. Let $v_p(n)$ denote the exponent of a prime $p$ in the prime factorization of $n$.
For any prime $p$, let the exponents of $p$ in the numbers on the board be $e_1, e_2, \dots, e_{2100}$.
The operation replaces two exponents $x, y$ with $\min(x, y)$ and $\max(x, y)$.
This operation is equivalent to sorting the multiset of exponents. Repeatedly applying this operation to any pair will eventually result in the entire multiset of exponents being sorted in non-decreasing order for each prime independently.
Since the choices of pairs can be made arbitrarily, Mark can effectively sort the vector of exponents for every prime $p$ simultaneously. The final set of numbers will consist of 2100 integers $n_1, n_2, \dots, n_{2100}$ such that for every prime $p$, the sequence of exponents $v_p(n_1), v_p(n_2), \dots, v_p(n_{2100})$ is non-decreasing.
This implies that if we sort the final numbers in increasing order, say $N_1 < N_2 < \dots < N_{2100}$, then for any $i < j$, $N_i$ divides $N_j$. This is because $v_p(N_i) \le v_p(N_j)$ for all primes $p$.
Thus, the final numbers form a chain under divisibility.

Let's look at the initial set of numbers $\{1, 2, \dots, 2100\}$.
For a specific prime $p$, let $E_p = \{v_p(1), v_p(2), \dots, v_p(2100)\}$ be the multiset of exponents.
The final number $N_k$ (the $k$-th smallest) will have the exponent for prime $p$ equal to the $k$-th smallest element in the sorted list of $E_p$.
